title: The Ark Leads Israel Across the Jordan
summary: Israel moves from Shittim to the bank of the Jordan and waits three days. Joshua tells the people to follow the ark of the covenant at a distance and to consecrate themselves for the wonders the LORD will do. When the priests carrying the ark step into the flooded river, the water upstream stops and piles up at the town of Adam, and the whole nation crosses on dry ground while the priests stand in the middle of the riverbed.
story: The spies have returned with news that the land's inhabitants are melting in fear. Now comes the moment the whole Pentateuch has been leading toward: Israel enters the land promised to Abraham. The crossing echoes the Red Sea crossing forty years earlier (Exodus 14), when the parents of this generation walked through the sea on dry ground. That generation died in the wilderness; this one receives its own miracle. The chapter also fulfills God's promise in 1:5 and confirms Joshua as Moses' successor: the LORD says he will exalt Joshua so that Israel will know he is with him as he was with Moses (verse 7). Chapter 4 will describe the memorial stones and the completion of the crossing.
historical:
Israel crosses opposite Jericho, in the lower Jordan valley north of the Dead Sea. The Jordan here is not wide, but in spring, fed by melting snow from Mount Hermon and the winter rains, it could overflow its banks and become a dangerous torrent spreading across the flood plain (verse 15). The narrator's note that this was harvest season, confirmed in 4:19 as the tenth day of the first month (early spring), heightens the miracle: the river was at its fullest.

The water stopped at Adam, a town near Zarethan (verse 16). Adam is usually identified with Tell ed-Damiyeh, near where the Jabbok River joins the Jordan, some distance upstream from Jericho. Interestingly, landslides from the high clay banks near this site are reported to have blocked the Jordan for hours on several occasions, including in the thirteenth century AD and during an earthquake in 1927. Some readers see this as the natural means God used, with the timing as the miracle. Others insist the text describes an event beyond any natural explanation. Either way, the text presents the crossing as the LORD's act, done at the moment the priests' feet touched the water.
cultural:
The ark of the covenant was a wooden chest overlaid with gold, containing the stone tablets of the covenant, with a cover flanked by two cherubim (Exodus 25:10-22). It represented the LORD's throne or footstool and his presence among his people. The Levitical priests carried it on poles, and no one else was to touch it (Numbers 4:15). Keeping a distance of about two thousand cubits (roughly half a mile, since a cubit was about eighteen inches) had two effects: it showed reverence for God's holiness, and it allowed the whole people to see the ark and follow where it led (verse 4).

To consecrate oneself (verse 5) meant to prepare ritually for an encounter with God, which in Exodus 19:10-15 included washing clothes and abstaining from sexual relations. The list of seven peoples in verse 10 (Canaanites, Hittites, Hivites, Perizzites, Girgashites, Amorites, and Jebusites) is a standard formula in the Pentateuch for the inhabitants of the land. Some of these groups are known from outside the Bible, while others are known only from Scripture. The number seven may itself signal completeness.
literary: The chapter is built around repeated movement toward a single moment: the priests' feet touching the water. The narrator slows down, repeating instructions (the ark, the priests, the distance, the twelve men) and building anticipation through three days of waiting, a night of consecration, and speeches by the officers, Joshua, and the LORD. Key words recur: to cross or pass over (abar) appears again and again, and the ark is mentioned ten times. God is called the living God and “the Lord of all the earth” (verses 10, 11, 13), a title that claims authority over the land and its rivers, which Canaanite religion might attribute to Baal or to the river itself. The chapter ends with a still picture: the priests standing firm on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan while all Israel passes by. The account continues directly into chapter 4, which retells parts of the crossing from another angle.

outline.t: Camping at the Jordan and orders to follow the ark
Consecrate yourselves; the priests go ahead
Joshua announces the sign of the living God
The waters stop and Israel crosses on dry ground

doctrines.note: The LORD is the living God and the Lord of all the earth. He rules the river, the land, and the peoples in it, and he shows this by acting in history for his people.
The people must consecrate themselves and keep their distance from the ark. God's presence is gracious and near, leading them forward, but it is also holy and not to be treated casually.
The waters do not stop until the priests step in. Faith here is obedience in advance of seeing, entering the flood on the strength of God's word.

words.note: Abar, to cross, pass over, or go beyond. It is the chapter's key verb, used again and again for Israel crossing the Jordan. The same root gives the word Hebrew (ivri), which may originally have meant one from beyond or across, though that connection is debated.

Aron, chest or ark. Here it is the ark of the covenant, the visible sign of God's presence. In Joshua 3 and 4 it leads the people, stands in the river, and holds the waters back. It is not a magic object; its power lies in the God whose presence it represents, as Israel will learn painfully in 1 Samuel 4.

Ned, heap. The waters stand up in a heap (verses 13, 16). The same rare word is used in the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:8) for the waters of the Red Sea standing up, deliberately linking the two crossings.

Gadal, to be great, or in this form to make great or exalt. God will exalt Joshua (verse 7) so the people will know he is with him. Joshua's authority comes from God's action, not from self-promotion.

christ: The crossing of the Jordan became, in later Jewish and Christian imagination, a picture of passing from one life into another. The New Testament does not directly interpret Joshua 3, but it does draw on the pattern of which it is part. Paul describes Israel's passage through the Red Sea as a baptism into Moses (1 Corinthians 10:1-2), and the Jordan crossing repeats that pattern. It is also in the Jordan that John baptizes and Jesus himself is baptized (Matthew 3:13-17), beginning his public ministry at the place where Israel first entered the land. Whether the Gospel writers intended an echo of Joshua is debated, but the location is suggestive: the one who bears Joshua's name enters his work where Joshua entered the land. Christian hymns and spirituals have often used crossing the Jordan as an image of death and entry into God's final rest, a reading that belongs to later devotion rather than to the chapter itself.

hard.q: Did the Jordan really stop flowing, and how should we understand the miracle?
hard.a: Readers take different approaches. Many conservative interpreters understand the event as a direct supernatural act in which God stopped the river at the moment the priests entered it, just as the text says. Others note the reports of landslides near Tell ed-Damiyeh that have blocked the river for hours in recorded history and suggest that God may have used such an event, with the miracle lying in its timing and in its connection to the ark and God's announced word. Critical scholars often view the account as a liturgical or theological retelling shaped to mirror the exodus, perhaps connected to later worship at Gilgal, and are less concerned with reconstructing the physical event. What the text itself emphasizes is not the mechanism but the meaning: the living God, Lord of all the earth, opened the way into the land as he had opened the sea.

questions: The priests had to step into the flooded river before the water stopped. Where might God be asking you to take a step before you can see how things will work out?
Israel was told to keep a distance from the ark so they could see where to go. How does reverence for God help you find your way?
This generation received its own crossing, echoing what God had done for their parents. How has God shown himself to you in ways that echo his work in earlier generations?
